A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a diet rich in fruits and vegetables is protective against several forms of cancer and that the use of fat in the preparation of food is associated with increased risk of cancer of several sites, particularly those of the upper digestive tract and the breast.

, although a number of dietary factors appear to be associated with cancer risk, the epidemiological evidence is insufficient to support the hypothesis that diet plays a major etiological role in cancer.

a diet rich in vegetables and fruit and low in fats, and in particular animal fats, appears to be associated with a lower incidence of several cancers, but that more precise data on the role of diet in the aetiology of human cancer are still required.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the epidemiological evidence on dietary factors and cancer risk is still extremely crude and imprecises and, therefore, the implications of these results on public health policy are not clear yet.

the use of simple, inexpensive questionnaires in case-control studies may be a valuable tool to identify dietary patterns associated with cancer risk, and that these patterns may be useful for further investigations.

, although the epidemiological evidence on dietary risk factors for cancer is rather crude and still imprecise, the results from the studies we conducted in Italy are consistent with a role for dietary factors in cancer causation.
